description:
We are Adeptus Vulkanis — three AI/ML engineers, one full-stack developer, and four massive Warhammer nerds.

We love ambitious projects, solving hard problems, and Warhammer probably more than is reasonable. Now we’re building Vulkan’s Watch to bring two satellite sensors into one clear picture of fire activity.

Vulkan lives. Into the fires of data, unto the anvil of code.
summary: Ember Almanac answers one question for any of 159 countries and Texas: did fire activity really change, or did our satellites just get better at seeing it? In 2012 the sharper VIIRS sensor joined MODIS, so raw fire counts jump for technical reasons. Our team harmonized NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS detections into one consistent record from 2000 to November 2026 and built a web app around it. Its home screen is a burning calendar — years by months — where any month can be clicked to get a plain sentence such as "×0.5 vs median of 25 Octobers, preliminary". Every number carries its status (checked, estimate, preliminary, no data), and missing data is never shown as zero. A 3D satellite map shows where fire was detected, a statistical test says whether there is a trend, and a CSV export keeps all statuses. The app works in English, Russian and Tajik, so fire services in Central Asia can use it directly.
details:
Ember Almanac turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS hot spots into a calendar that anyone can read. Pick a country (search in English, Russian or Tajik, or use your location), click a month, and the app tells you how that month compares with the usual one, how sure it is, and where the fires were.

How it works

  • Our data team harmonized MODIS and VIIRS: years before VIIRS are rescaled into VIIRS units, static sources such as gas flares are removed, and activity is counted as fire-days on an H3 hexagon grid. They serve it with a Python/FastAPI service (pandas, H3, Docker).
  • The web app (Next.js 16, TypeScript, MapLibre, ECharts) computes everything users read: the usual month is the median of the same month in at least 10 other years, never including the year itself; trends use the Mann–Kendall test with a Theil–Sen slope, and we say "no detectable trend" when p ≥ 0.05.
  • The expected range for the next six months is shown as a range, labelled "not a forecast", together with how often past months actually fell inside it (in Kazakhstan, 78% for the 80% range).
  • The map shows fire locations for each of the last 12 months, or a typical year, over satellite imagery with 3D relief.

Benefits and impact

Fire and forestry services get one honest sentence per month instead of millions of dots, and can tell a real change from a sensor change. Tajik and Russian interfaces make it usable in Central Asia, where such tools are usually English-only.
